section.name: Subscription Model
section.t: Subscribers SHOULD subscribe to the source track first, then subscribe to the repair track if:

ol.li: The track's catalog entry signals FEC (a fec object naming a repairTrack, Section 5.1), AND
The subscriber desires FEC protection

section.t: Repair-track subscription is selective and per-need: a subscriber chooses whether to consume repair data based on its own path conditions, and MAY start or stop its repair-track subscription at any time during the session -- for example, subscribing only after observing loss, or not subscribing at all on a reliable path.

Publishers and relays MUST NOT require subscription to repair tracks and MUST NOT condition delivery of a source track on a repair-track subscription. Repair tracks are optional; subscribers MAY choose to rely solely on QUIC retransmission or to accept unrecovered loss.

section.name: Layered Repair Tracks
section.t: A source track MAY be protected by more than one repair track. Each such track is a repair layer: an independently subscribable set of repair symbols for the same source blocks. Layer 0 is the repair track named by repairTrack, carrying the source's repairSymbols symbols per block. Layers 1..n are the tracks that name this source in depends and carry a repairLayer (Section 5.1.1), one track per layer index.

Layered repair is an extension of that an ISO AL-FEC message cannot express: each FEC source flow has one FEC encoded flow, whose one-stage coding structure carries a single repair_flow_id ( Clause C.6.3), so only layer 0 maps to an ISO repair flow. An in-band AL-FEC message names layer 0 and no other layer ( Section 8.3). A repair layer is also unrelated to the layers of ISO layer-aware FEC (LA-FEC, Clause C.2.3).

Layering separates the two costs of FEC: the repair count P buys tolerance to random loss at a cost in bandwidth, and the interleave window buys tolerance to burst loss at a cost in recovery latency (Section 9). Layers let a receiver on a lossier path add repair without changing the source encoding. A source track names only layer 0; each further layer declares itself on its own tracks entry, so the layer set is validated as a whole (Section 6.3.4) and changed only as Section 6.3.9 allows. A relay that forwards a subset of a catalog MUST NOT forward a fec-repair track whose source track it does not forward (Section 6.3.4, rule 9).

section.name: Shared Block Geometry
section.t: All repair layers of a source track share its block geometry (algorithm, blockProfile, sourceSymbols, symbolSize, interleaveDepthMs, reorderToleranceMs) and differ only in repairSymbols. A repair layer MUST NOT carry a geometry field; rule 8 of Section 6.3.4 lists them, and a receiver rejects a catalog that violates it. Because each source packet carries one base Source FEC Payload ID (Section 8.5), a different K or interleave window needs a separate rendition; the keyframe overlay (Section 6.4) is a separate FEC instance, not a layer.

section.name: Repair Symbol Identity Across Layers
section.t: Let P_i be the repairSymbols of layer i and O_i its RS_ID offset, defined below (O_0 = 0). P_0 is the source track's fec.repairSymbols (Section 6.3.4, rule 11), and P_i for i >= 1 the layer track's own repairSymbols. Layer i carries, for every source block, the repair symbols with RS_ID in [O_i, O_i + P_i). The Encoding Symbol ID follows the single-layer rule of Section 7.2:
section.artwork: O_i = sum(P_j for j < i) RS_ID = O_i + j, for the j-th symbol of layer i ESI = SSB_length + RS_ID
section.t: where SSB_length is the block's source symbol count (Section 7.1).

The total repair count of the block is the sum of P_i over all published layers. RSB_length on every repair packet of every layer carries this total (Section 7.1), not the layer's own P_i. That is what makes the RS_ID to ESI mapping independent of which layers a given receiver joined: a receiver holding a non-prefix subset computes the same coordinate for a symbol as a receiver holding everything, and the RS_ID < RSB_length bound holds for a symbol from any layer.

Because RaptorQ repair symbols are identified by ESI alone and any set of distinct encoding symbols of a block decodes together (), symbols received from any subset of layers, over any mix of paths, combine in one decode. Subsets need not be prefixes: in the worked catalog of Section 5.1.2 a receiver holding layers 0 and 2 holds, for a full block, ESIs 64 to 71 and 88 to 119, which are distinct encoding symbols of one code, and it decodes as soon as it holds enough distinct symbols in total.

A receiver that has subscribed a set of layers recovers a block whenever the number of lost symbols, source and repair together, does not exceed C - e, where C is the total P over the layers it holds and e is the RaptorQ decoding overhead (roughly 1e-2, 1e-4, and 1e-6 residual failure at 0, 1, and 2 symbols of overhead per ). This loss tolerance is derived from K and the layer counts; it MUST NOT be signaled as a separate catalog field.
Receivers MUST take layer membership and per-layer counts from the catalog. RSB_length carries the total and says nothing about which layers a receiver holds.

On layer i, the block's repair objects form the MoQ group whose Group ID is the block's extended SS_Start (Section 7.5), and that group carries P_i objects (Section 7); object j of that group carries the repair symbol with RS_ID = O_i + j.

section.name: Why RaptorQ Only
section.t: Repair layers and the overlay are defined only for raptorq: a publisher MUST NOT signal either under any other algorithm, and a receiver rejects such a catalog (Section 6.3.4, rule 7). Layering relies on RaptorQ's open Encoding Symbol ID space, in which repair symbols from disjoint ESI ranges on separate tracks remain symbols of one code; a block code such as Reed-Solomon fixes n = K + P at encoding time, so its symbols for one P are not valid for another.

section.name: Catalog Rules and Fail-Closed Validation
section.t: A receiver MUST validate all of the following for a source track before starting FEC for it. On any violation the receiver MUST fail closed: it MUST report the offending catalog path and MUST NOT start FEC for that source track. A receiver MUST NOT repair the catalog by ignoring the offending track, because every rule below distinguishes a layer set that decodes from one that silently mis-maps symbols.

ol.li: depends names exactly one track in the same catalog, whose packaging is mmtp and which carries an fec object.
The repairLayer values for one source track are contiguous from 1 to n, with no gaps and no duplicates. Layer 0 is the track named by the source's fec.repairTrack.
priority, where declared, is in the range 192 to 255 inclusive, and is monotonic non-decreasing with layer index. Layer 0's priority MAY be declared on its own track; when absent it is 240.
For each FEC instance, the total of repairSymbols across all its layers is at most 2^24 - 1, the range of RSB_length.
For each FEC instance, K + totalP - 1 is at most 2^24 - 1, which bounds the largest ESI the instance can produce.

For each FEC instance, K is at most 56403. extends a source block of K source symbols to K' symbols, the smallest value at least K in its Table 2 ( Section 5.3.1), and 56403 is the largest such value, K'_max ( Section 5.1.2), so a RaptorQ source block holds at most 56403 source symbols.
Repair layers and any overlay appear only when fec.algorithm is raptorq (Section 6.3.3 above).

A track whose packaging is fec-repair carries no geometry field, whether as a flat field or inside an fec object of its own: algorithm, blockProfile, mmtpMode, timescale, any groupDuration field, symbolSize, interleaveDepthMs, reorderToleranceMs, and sourceSymbols except on an overlay (Section 6.4).

No orphan repair track: every track whose packaging is fec-repair is reachable from a source track, either by being named in that source's fec.repairTrack or by naming that source in depends. This rule binds once the catalog declares any FEC source, that is any track whose fec.algorithm is not none; a catalog that declares no FEC source at all MAY carry an unreferenced fec-repair track that nothing joins. This rule is the one exception to the per-source remedy of the preamble above: an orphan track is by definition associated with no source track, so there is no source track to stop. The receiver MUST refuse to join the orphan track and MUST report its catalog path, and MUST NOT stop FEC for any source track on account of it.
A source track has at most one track with "scope": "keyframe" (Section 6.4), and such a track carries no repairLayer.

The layer-0 repair track's repairSymbols, where declared, equals the source track's fec.repairSymbols. The source field is the single authoritative value of P_0; the layer-0 track MAY restate it and MUST restate it identically. A receiver MUST reject a catalog declaring both with different values, and MUST NOT resolve the conflict by preferring either field, because the two readings disagree about O_1, about the block total, and therefore about the RSB_length that every layer's packets carry (Section 6.3.2). This rule is why rules 4 and 5 have a single well defined totalP to bound.

section.t: Section 6.3.9 adds one check that can only be made on received repair packets.

The following are the fail-closed cases this section introduces, written against the worked catalog of Section 5.1.2 (K = 64, P_0 = 8, P_1 = 16, P_2 = 32) so that each defect is one edit away from a valid catalog. Each row violates the rule shown, and none of them is detectable from the wire.

tr.th: Why the wire cannot catch it

tr.td: video/repair declares repairSymbols 16 while the source declares fec.repairSymbols 8

Both readings are self-consistent: one derives O_1 = 8 and total 56, the other O_1 = 16 and total 64. A repair symbol is identified by ESI alone, so a receiver that resolved P_0 the other way decodes with a shifted mapping and reports a corrupt block, not a catalog error.
Both claim RS_ID 8 to 23. Symbols from the two tracks are distinct on the wire but collide in ESI, so a decode fed from both sees duplicate encoding symbols and stalls short of K.
video/repair/2 is present but no track declares layer 1
O_2 is a function of P_1, which is absent, so the receiver has no offset for layer 2 at all.
The overlay is a second FEC instance over its own K (Section 6.4). Admitting it as a layer would fold its RS_ID space into O_i and place its symbols in the base instance's ESI range.
A second track for video declares "scope": "keyframe"
A RAP packet carries one overlay SS_ID, in its one header extension (Section 8.5.1), so a second overlay has no SS_ID on the wire.
video/repair/1 carries symbolSize or its own fec object
A repair track carrying its own geometry would name itself as layer 0 and bypass rule 9's reachability check.

section.t: A receiver MAY report several violations at once.

section.name: Receiver Selection
section.t: The per-need model of Section 6.2 applies to each layer independently. On a lossy path a receiver SHOULD subscribe layer 0 first. When a block fails recovery with the receiver's current layer set and a higher layer exists, the receiver SHOULD subscribe the next layer; it MAY instead request only the failed block's repair objects from that layer, a request bounded to the block's repair group (Section 7.5), when the block is still inside its recovery budget (Section 9). On a multicast or AMT leg, Section 11.4 governs such per-block requests: which blocks get one, when, with what budget and priority, and what happens when one fails. A receiver MAY unsubscribe a layer after a receiver-chosen number of consecutive blocks whose loss stayed within the tolerance of the remaining layers. Hysteresis is counted in blocks, the protocol's unit, not by a fixed timer (Section 6.3.6).

section.name: Repair-Only Multicast Endpoints
section.t: On a multicast endpoint the receiver cannot choose tracks; the operator of the endpoint chooses which tracks that path carries. Each repair layer carried on an endpoint is listed with its own packetId ( Section 4.1), exactly as a source track is, and a receiver MUST route every such packetId to the decoder of the source track that layer depends on. Because every endpoint carries the same source packets under the same block partition (Section 6.3.1), a receiver that moves between endpoints, or that is side-fed over MoQ unicast, mixes symbols from all of them in one decode. Layers not carried on any endpoint the receiver holds remain reachable over MoQ unicast (Section 6.2) for receivers that have a return path.

An operator MAY carry the source track and its layers together on one endpoint, or MAY place layers on endpoints of their own. An endpoint whose track list contains only fec-repair tracks is a repair-only endpoint:

The first endpoint suits a regional path with low random loss. The second is repair-only: a receiver on a lossy path holds both, and receives source packets once while adding layers 1 and 2 to the same decode.

A repair-only endpoint is never a media tier. A receiver MUST NOT treat one as a rendition or quality choice, and endpoint or ladder selection MUST exclude it on every path by which a receiver picks what to render. A repair-only endpoint's bandwidth ( Section 4.1) is the cost of adding repair to a stream the receiver has already selected, not the cost of an alternative rendition, and MUST NOT be compared against a media endpoint's bandwidth when choosing one.

A receiver joins a repair-only endpoint on measured loss: the rate at which its FEC blocks fail to recover, and the margin by which recovering blocks consume the repair symbols available to it. A receiver MUST NOT use goodput, throughput, or estimated available bandwidth to decide whether to add or drop a repair layer.

Layer changes are make-before-break. A receiver MUST join the additional layer's endpoint and begin receiving from it before leaving any endpoint it currently holds, so that no source block is left with less coverage than the receiver already had.

Hysteresis MUST derive from the FEC block span, that is from interleaveDepthMs together with reorderToleranceMs, and MUST NOT come from a fixed timer or a fixed symbol count. A receiver MUST observe at least one full block span at the new layer set before making a further layer change.

section.name: Interaction with the Interleave Window
section.t: Layers never change interleaveDepthMs, the stream's single recovery-latency lever (Section 9). A shallow window recovers bursts only by per-block unicast repair (Sections 6.3.5 and 11.4.2), at about one round trip; a deep window recovers them in band at that window's latency. Serving both requires two renditions (Section 6.3.1).

section.name: Compatibility
section.t: A source track with a single repair track is the one-layer case (O_0 = 0, RSB_length = repairSymbols). A receiver that subscribes only layer 0 decodes correctly whatever other layers exist: layer 0 alone is a valid layer set, and it uses RSB_length only as the RS_ID < RSB_length bound. The keyframe overlay is the exception: a receiver has to recognize its declaration, because its repair packets belong to another FEC instance (Section 6.4.3).

section.name: Changing the Layer Set Within a Session
section.t: Publishing a layer is adding one tracks entry and withdrawing it is removing one, but the two directions are not symmetric, because O_i is a function of every lower layer's P (Section 6.3.2). A change to the set can therefore move the coordinates of a layer a receiver has already joined. This subsection states which changes are defined.

Layer sets are append-only. A publisher MAY append a layer at the next index above the highest published one. It MUST NOT withdraw a published layer, at any index, for the lifetime of the source encoding. An append changes O_i for no layer already published, because no published layer's set of lower layers changes. It does raise the total, so RSB_length on the wire rises, which is benign for the reason Section 6.3.8 gives: a receiver uses the total only as the RS_ID < RSB_length bound, so a receiver holding a catalog from before an append reads a smaller bound that excludes only symbols of layers it has not joined.

A publisher MUST NOT renumber the repairLayer of a published layer, and MUST NOT change the repairSymbols of a published layer, while any receiver may still be consuming the source track. Rule 2 of Section 6.3.4 requires repairLayer to be contiguous from 1 to n, so withdrawing a layer that is not the highest would force exactly such a renumbering. A publisher that must retire any layer, including the highest, retires the source encoding and publishes a separate rendition. Supporting withdrawal directly would require a catalog generation identifier carried on the wire, that is in-session signaling, which Section 5.2 does not define.

The prohibition is not editorial, and the worked catalog of Section 5.1.2 shows why. A receiver holding layers 0 and 2 holds, for a full block, ESIs 64 to 71 and 88 to 119. Renumber layer 2 to layer 1 and the same track's offset becomes O = 8, so the publisher now labels those symbols ESI 72 to 103 while the receiver still maps them to 88 to 119. The receiver feeds correctly received symbols into the decoder under wrong coordinates. RaptorQ does not detect this, because a repair symbol is identified by its ESI alone: the result is not a reported error but a decode that fails, or that resolves against coordinates the symbols do not belong to. Changing a published repairSymbols does the same to every layer above the one changed.

Withdrawing the highest layer forces no renumbering, but it is barred for a different reason: it is indistinguishable on the wire from the renumbering above. For the highest layer n, O_n + P_n is the total identically, so withdrawing it drops the wire RSB_length strictly below the bound derived by every receiver that had joined it, and the check below cannot tell that case from a genuine coordinate disagreement. Both present as nothing but a smaller total. The receivers holding the highest layer are also the lossiest ones, and they cannot recover by observation: absence of symbols is precisely the loss condition the layer was joined to repair, so they learn of the withdrawal only at the next catalog refresh, which this document does not bound.

Append-only is what makes the check below sound. RSB_length is monotonically non-decreasing over the lifetime of a source encoding, so a wire RSB_length below a held layer's O_i + P_i is always a genuine violation: no operation this document defines produces one.

A receiver MUST fail closed when, for any layer i it holds, the RSB_length carried on any repair packet of the same FEC instance is less than O_i + P_i derived from its own catalog: its own layer's RS_ID range does not fit under the bound the publisher is advertising, so the two disagree about coordinates the receiver is actively using. It MUST NOT treat such a packet as a symbol to discard. In the renumbering example above the total falls from 56 to 40 while the receiver's O_2 + P_2 is 56, so the check catches it.

That check is a backstop and not a substitute for the publisher requirement. It does not catch a change that leaves the total at or above the receiver's derived bound, for example an increase to a lower layer's repairSymbols, which shifts every higher offset while raising the total. That case is silent on the wire, which is why the protection is the prohibition on the publisher rather than validation at the receiver. A wire RSB_length larger than the receiver's derived total is not an error in itself: that is the append case above.

section.name: Keyframe Overlay
section.t: A source track MAY additionally be protected by a keyframe overlay: a second, independent FEC instance whose source symbols are only the fragments of Random Access Points of that source track.

Losing part of a Random Access Point makes every dependent frame undecodable until the next one; the overlay protects RAP fragments across a block of its own, which can be wider than the base window, without changing the base instance's latency.

section.name: Overlay Instance
section.t: An overlay is a separate FEC instance over the same source track. It has its own sourceSymbols (K_overlay) and its own repairSymbols, declared on its own repair track, and it shares the source track's algorithm, blockProfile and symbolSize. It does not share the base instance's K, its block partition, its SS_ID space, or its RS_ID space.

Every per-block quantity of this document -- K, the total repair count P, SS_ID, ESI, RS_ID, SS_Start, RSB_length, SSB_length, the short-block rules of Section 7.4, the wrap epoch and repair group IDs of Section 7.5, and the bounds of Section 6.3.4 -- is defined within one FEC instance. For the base instance, K is the source track's fec.sourceSymbols and P is the sum of repairSymbols over its published layers (Section 6.3.2); for an overlay, K and P are the sourceSymbols and repairSymbols of its own track. A repair packet belongs to the instance of the track it arrived on (Section 6.4.2).

An overlay is not a repair layer. It carries no repairLayer, it is not a member of the layer index chain, and it is excluded from the contiguity and priority monotonicity rules of Section 6.3.4, which order the base layer chain only. Its priority is independent within 192 to 255, and MAY be numerically lower than a base enhancement layer's so that a keyframe repair symbol is delivered before an ordinary one.

Overlay ESIs never collide with base ESIs because the two are different instances decoded by different decoders; a receiver MUST NOT feed a repair symbol of one instance to the decoder of the other, and MUST NOT reuse a source symbol's coordinate in one instance as its coordinate in the other. A RAP source packet is a source symbol of both instances, at an unrelated coordinate in each (Section 6.4.2).

A source track has at most one overlay (Section 6.3.4, rule 10), a wire constraint explained in Section 8.5.1. An overlay is declared only by the catalog, never in an in-band AL-FEC message, and only where no FEC source or repair packet carries FFSRP_TS (Section 8.5.1).

section.name: Overlay Membership
section.t: The overlay's source symbols are the fragments of the source track that belong to a Random Access Point, in transmission order. A publisher that declares an overlay MUST set RAP_flag on a source packet of the track, MUST include the packet in the overlay instance, and MUST carry the packet's overlay SS_ID in its 0x8B01 header extension (Section 8.5.1), if and only if that packet's payload belongs to a keyframe MFU covered by the overlay.

Overlay source symbols are numbered consecutively within the overlay instance, in the order the publisher emits them: the overlay SS_ID is 0 at the first overlay source symbol of the stream and advances by one per overlay source symbol, modulo 2^32 (Section 7.5). It is the value the RAP source packet carries in its 0x8B01 header extension (Section 8.5.1). It lives in the overlay instance's own SS_ID space, independent of the base instance's, and the two IDs on one packet are unrelated numbers. An overlay source block holds at most K_overlay overlay source symbols, and overlay blocks, including short ones, are formed, located and wrapped exactly as base blocks are (Sections 7.4, 7.5 and 8.3), with K_overlay as the upper bound on their SSB_length. Because a RAP is a small fraction of the media, an overlay block spans many base blocks; the overlay's recovery latency is therefore its own block span and is unrelated to interleaveDepthMs.

A receiver knows that a source packet is an overlay source symbol because the packet carries the 0x8B01 header extension (Section 8.5.1). It knows that a repair packet belongs to the overlay because it arrives on the repair track that the catalog declares with "scope": "keyframe" for this source track, and that track has its own packet_id. The instance is therefore fixed by the track the packet arrived on; no field of the repair packet distinguishes the two, and a receiver MUST NOT attempt to infer the instance from SS_Start, RSB_length, or SSB_length, whose values are only interpretable once the instance is known.

section.name: Receiver Behavior
section.t: A receiver that implements overlays and has joined the overlay repair track decodes the two instances independently and MAY use the recovered RAP fragments even when the base instance failed to recover the block that carried them.

The overlay is the publisher-side half of keyframe protection. The receiver-side half is the repair policy of Section 11.4, under which a receiver gives a keyframe-bearing base block that in-band decoding leaves unrecovered priority unicast repair; Section 11.4.6 states how the two combine.

A receiver that does not implement overlays MUST fail closed on a catalog that declares one for a track it intends to consume, that is on a fec-repair track carrying the unknown scope key, and MUST NOT ignore the key and consume the source track anyway. This is one of the unknown-key exceptions of Section 5.1.1: a receiver that ignored the key could not tell the overlay's repair track from a repair layer of the base instance, and would feed the base decoder repair symbols of another FEC instance (Section 6.4.2).

This mechanism is not backward compatible with receivers that predate it, for the same reason. A publisher that must serve such receivers publishes the overlay on a separate source track, or does not publish it.

section.name: Repair Object Header
section.t: Each object on a repair track is one complete MMTP repair packet (packet type 0x03, FEC Type 2) carrying exactly one repair symbol. Its layout is the ISO 23008-1 AL-FEC repair packet form -- the MMTP packet header followed by the 13-byte Repair FEC Payload ID and the repair symbol data ( Sections C.4.3 and C.5.3; ssbg_mode1, one-stage FEC with N = 1, and ffsrpts_flag = 0, so no FFSRP_TS, Section C.5.1) -- so the same repair packet is valid on MoQ, multicast UDP, and native broadcast paths without translation, and matches the repair-object depiction of Section 7. The layout below reproduces Section C.5.3 for convenience:

MMTP Packet Header: The standard 12-byte MMTP packet header ( Section 3.1) with packet type 0x03 (repair) and FEC Type 2; its packet_id routes the repair flow. Like every packet of its MMTP packet flow, source and signaling packets included, a repair packet has the packet counter flag C = 0 ( Section 3.1; Clause 9.2.3). A repair packet MUST NOT carry a header extension (X = 0). Because C = 0 and X = 0, the Repair FEC Payload ID always begins at byte offset 12.

SS_Start (32 bits): The SS_ID of the first source symbol of the protected source block ( Section C.5.3). The blocks of an FEC instance are consecutive: the block after this one starts at SS_Start + SSB_length, modulo 2^32 (Section 7.4), so this block is the SS_ID range [SS_Start, SS_Start + SSB_length) and is identified by its SS_Start. Extended to 62 bits, SS_Start is also the MoQ Group ID of the block's repair objects (Section 7.5). Every field below is that of the packet's FEC instance (Section 6.4.1).
RSB_length (24 bits): The number of repair symbols generated for the block: the instance's total repair count P, identical on every repair packet of the instance; a layer does not carry its own P_i.

RS_ID (24 bits): The zero-based index of this repair symbol among the block's P repair symbols. The RFC 6330 Encoding Symbol ID is derived as ESI = SSB_length + RS_ID (Section 7.2). Layer i of the base instance carries RS_ID in [O_i, O_i + P_i) (Section 6.3.2).

The encoder performs one RaptorQ encoding pass per source block of each instance, producing the total repair count, and then assigns the disjoint RS_ID ranges to the layer tracks according to O_i. It MUST NOT run a separate encoding per layer: separate encodings of the same block are not symbols of a single code, so they could not be combined by a receiver holding more than one layer, which is the property Section 6.3.2 depends on.

SSB_length (24 bits): The number of source symbols in the protected source block ( Section C.5.3), from 1 to K, where K is the instance's sourceSymbols (Section 5.1); it is K for a full block. It is authoritative for the block: the block is a RaptorQ source block of SSB_length source symbols, its repair ESIs start at SSB_length (Section 7.2), and its decoder is configured with F = SSB_length x T (Section 4.2). A value below K marks a short source block, to which this document's framing adds no padding symbols (Section 7.4). A publisher MUST NOT send 0 or a value above K; a receiver discards a repair packet carrying either (Section 7.4).

Repair Symbol Data: Exactly one repair symbol of Symbol Size (T) bytes, generated per Section 7.2. Carrying one symbol per object aligns the loss unit with the FEC symbol (Section 11.3) and requires no symbol-count field.

section.name: Repair Symbols
section.t: For RaptorQ, repair symbols are generated per Section 5.3. The source symbols of a block occupy ESIs 0 to SSB_length - 1 in SS_ID order, and the Encoding Symbol ID (ESI) of a repair symbol starts at SSB_length, the block's K in the notation of ( Section 5.3.1): ESI = SSB_length + RS_ID, both fields taken from the Repair FEC Payload ID (Section 7.1). The Internal Symbol IDs of , which start the repair symbols at that document's K', are internal to its encoder and decoder and never appear on the wire.
Repair symbol generation for extension algorithms (Section 4.3) is not specified by this document.

section.name: Sub-Blocks and ssbg_mode
section.t: Per ISO 23008-1 Section C.3.3 (signalled per C.6.3, Table C.5), the FEC block structure is described by the source symbol block generation (SSBG) mode (ssbg_mode). The iso-ssbg1-v1 block profile (Section 5.1) uses ssbg_mode1, with the one-stage FEC coding structure and FEC payload ID mode 0 ( Clause C.1).

ssbg_mode1: One MMTP source packet = one source symbol, which records the packet's length. Each MoQ object or multicast UDP datagram carries exactly one FEC symbol. Repair symbols are exactly T bytes on the wire; a SOURCE packet MAY be shorter than T on the wire -- the length field and the zero padding that complete its T-byte source symbol are applied by the encoder and decoder as part of the source symbol construction below and are NOT transmitted. This is the natural model for MMTP because packets are sized to fit in UDP datagrams and no fragmentation or reassembly is needed at the FEC layer. Every source symbol is exactly T bytes, so a block of SSB_length source symbols is exactly SSB_length x T bytes -- the property the derived Transfer Length of Section 4.2 relies on. This is ssbg_mode1 of , not ssbg_mode0, which carries no length and requires every packet of the flow to be exactly one symbol long.

Source symbol construction: The protected packet of an FEC source packet is the complete MMTP packet -- the MMTP packet header, including any header extension, followed by the MMTP payload -- before its 4-byte Source FEC Payload ID is appended ( Section C.4.2; Section 8.5). Its T-byte source symbol is ( Section C.3.3):

The Length field is in network byte order and every Padding octet is zero, so the largest protected packet a symbol can carry is T - 2 octets. A publisher MUST size every FEC source packet so that its protected packet does not exceed T - 2 octets. A receiver that observes a source packet whose protected packet exceeds T - 2 octets MUST NOT feed it to the decoder -- a truncated symbol would corrupt recovery for the entire block -- but MAY still deliver the packet as media. On a RAP packet under a keyframe overlay (Section 6.4), the base and the overlay instance form the symbol from the same protected packet, so the two protect one identical T-byte symbol.

Recovery yields the block's SSB_length source symbols. From each, the receiver takes the Length octets that follow the Length field as the recovered protected packet, and delivers that packet to the MMTP parser. A receiver MUST NOT deliver a recovered symbol whose Length is less than 12, the size in bytes of the MMTP packet header ( Section 3.1), or points past the end of the symbol, or whose Padding octets are not all zero: each means that the symbol is not the one the publisher encoded.

A recovered packet carries no Source FEC Payload ID, of either instance: the trailer is appended after FEC encoding and is not part of the protected packet. A receiver MUST NOT re-append a trailer before delivering the recovered packet to the MMTP parser, and MUST NOT expect the recovered bytes to end in a block coordinate. This holds identically for a symbol recovered by a keyframe overlay, which the receiver delivers as media on the strength of the overlay recovery alone. The 0x8B01 header extension of a RAP packet under an overlay (Section 8.5.1) is part of the protected packet, by contrast, and is recovered with it.

The packet's base SS_ID was in the trailer, and this document defines no mapping from an overlay coordinate to a base one: a receiver MUST NOT place an overlay-recovered symbol into a base source block unless it has determined that packet's base SS_ID independently. Absent that, an overlay recovery is usable as media but MUST NOT be counted toward base block recovery, and in particular MUST NOT be treated as reducing the number of erasures the base decoder still has to solve. The other direction needs no such determination, because a RAP packet recovered by the base instance still carries its overlay SS_ID (Section 8.5.1).

In-band signaling: An AL-FEC message ( Section 8.3) that describes a track under iso-ssbg1-v1 carries the coding byte 0x14: fec_coding_structure 0001 (one-stage), ssbg_mode 01, ffsrpts_flag 0 (no FFSRP_TS) and fec_payload_id_mode 0 (a Source FEC Payload ID is appended to every FEC source packet), in that bit order, per Table C.3 of as replaced by . A message carrying any other value for such a track contradicts the catalog (Section 5.2).

Sub-blocks: When a single source block produces a large number of source symbols, RFC 6330 permits dividing each block into N sub-blocks (the Number of Sub-Blocks field of the OTI). The derived OTI of Section 4.2 fixes N = 1, so catalog-signaled sessions do not use sub-blocks; sub-block operation by broadcast systems that carry an explicit OTI is described informatively in Section 12.2. A publisher using MMTP packaging under iso-ssbg1-v1 therefore uses ssbg_mode1 without sub-blocks, and never ssbg_mode2.

section.name: Short Source Blocks
section.t: A publisher MAY close a source block before it holds K source symbols, for example at a media-unit boundary so that the block's span stays within interleaveDepthMs (Section 5.1). Such a block is a short source block, and it is a block with a smaller source symbol count: every block holds SSB_length source symbols, 1 <= SSB_length <= K ( Section C.5.3), and K -- the catalog sourceSymbols, carried in band as maximum_k_for_repair_flow -- is an upper bound on SSB_length, not the size of any particular block. A short block differs from a full one only in SSB_length:

li.t: The publisher encodes the block as a RaptorQ source block of its SSB_length source symbols (F = SSB_length x T, Section 4.2), at ESIs 0 to SSB_length - 1 in SS_ID order, and MUST carry that count in the SSB_length field of every repair packet of the block, on every repair track of the instance. This document's framing adds no padding symbols to the block: none is transmitted, and none is counted in SSB_length or F. The padding of the block to K' symbols in the notation of ( Section 5.3.1) is part of RaptorQ encoding and decoding, performed inside the encoder and the decoder.
The next block starts at the SS_ID that follows the block's last source symbol: its SS_Start is SS_Start + SSB_length, modulo 2^32. No SS_ID is skipped, so every SS_ID belongs to exactly one block.
The block's repair ESIs start at SSB_length: ESI = SSB_length + RS_ID (Section 7.2).

The block is complete, and needs no repair, once the receiver holds all SSB_length of its source symbols. It is recoverable once the source and repair symbols the receiver holds together number at least SSB_length, plus the decoding overhead of Section 6.3.2.
Recovery yields the SSB_length source symbols, SSB_length x T bytes, each consumed per the source symbol construction of Section 7.3.

section.t: Source packets carry only SS_ID, so the (SS_Start, SSB_length) of a repair packet is the only wire signal of a block's extent. Until a receiver has accepted a repair packet of a block it knows neither: it holds the source packets of that block without placing them in any block (Section 8.3), and a run of SS_IDs that it does not hold is a run of lost source packets of one or more blocks it cannot yet delimit. It MUST NOT infer a block boundary, or SSB_length, from a gap in SS_IDs, from a group or MPU boundary, from elapsed time, or from sourceSymbols. A block all of whose repair packets are lost therefore remains undelimited until a repair packet of the block arrives, including one obtained by unicast repair (Section 11.4), which conveys (SS_Start, SSB_length) in the same way. When the receiver accepts a repair packet of a block that starts after the end of the blocks it has delimited, the SS_IDs between the two belong to one or more blocks of which it holds no repair packet.

A receiver MUST fail closed on inconsistent block signaling. It MUST discard a repair packet whose SSB_length is 0 or exceeds K. It MUST discard a repair packet whose SSB_length differs from the value it has already accepted for the block with the same SS_Start, and one whose range [SS_Start, SS_Start + SSB_length) overlaps a different block that it has already accepted, in each case leaving the state of every block unchanged.

section.name: SS_ID Wrap and Repair Group IDs
section.t: SS_ID and SS_Start are 32-bit values that start from an arbitrary value and wrap to 0 after their maximum ( Section C.5.2). Every comparison, distance and range test on them in this document, block membership (Section 8.3) included, uses serial number arithmetic with SERIAL_BITS = 32. A block can span the wrap: a block with SS_Start 2^32 - 3 and SSB_length 4 holds the SS_IDs 2^32 - 3, 2^32 - 2, 2^32 - 1 and 0, and the next block starts at SS_ID 1.

A MoQ Group ID is a 62-bit integer, and the groups of a track are ordered by it , so the repair objects of a block are grouped not under its 32-bit SS_Start, which wraps, but under its extended SS_Start:

wrap_epoch, from 0 to 2^30 - 1, counts the times that SS_Start has wrapped in the FEC instance before this block: it is 0 for the first block of the FEC instance's source encoding, and increases by one at each block whose SS_Start is numerically below its predecessor's. Equivalently, the ext(SS_Start) of a block is that of its predecessor plus the predecessor's SSB_length. On every repair track of the instance, the repair objects of a block form the MoQ Group whose Group ID is the block's ext(SS_Start) (Section 6.3.2). Repair Group IDs are therefore sparse, one per block at the block's first SS_ID, and strictly increasing.

A repair object received over MoQ thus carries its block's start twice: in the SS_Start of its Repair FEC Payload ID and in its Group ID. The SS_Start is authoritative. A receiver MUST discard a repair object whose Group ID modulo 2^32 differs from its SS_Start and, once it has established the wrap epoch, one whose Group ID differs from ext(SS_Start) or whose SS_Start it cannot extend (below), in each case leaving the state of every block unchanged. The Group ID of a discarded repair object is not a reference value r.
A receiver establishes the wrap epoch of an FEC instance in one of the following ways, and MUST NOT assume a wrap epoch that it has not established in one of them:

li.t: From the Group ID of a repair object of the instance that it has received over MoQ and not discarded (above). That Group ID is the reference value r. The publisher assigns it and MoQ delivers it unaltered, so it stands on the same footing as the Largest Location of way 2: the modulo 2^32 test above screens out an object to discard, and does not verify the epoch.

From the Largest Location that a TRACK_STATUS request for a repair track of the instance reports ( Section 9.13). The publisher answers TRACK_STATUS with a REQUEST_OK, which that document calls TRACK_STATUS_OK, carrying the parameters that it would set in a SUBSCRIBE_OK, among them the LARGEST_OBJECT parameter ( Section 9.20.18). The receiver reads the Group of the Location that LARGEST_OBJECT carries, whichever name the reply bears, and that Group is the reference value r. A reply without LARGEST_OBJECT reports a repair track on which no object has been published, and establishes no epoch.
As epoch 0, when the receiver has observed the instance from its first block, whose wrap_epoch is 0 (above). The reference value r is then that block's SS_Start.

section.t: A reference value r is an extended SS_Start, and the epoch is r shifted right by 32 bits. The receiver relates its own SS_IDs to it with serial arithmetic: it extends a later 32-bit SS_Start or SS_ID x relative to an extended value r that it already holds -- its reference value, or a value it extended before -- to the 62-bit value congruent to x modulo 2^32 that is nearest r in serial order: r advanced by the serial distance from the low 32 bits of r to x when x follows them, r moved back by the serial distance from x to them when x precedes them, and r itself when the two are equal. A receiver MUST NOT extend an x that lies exactly 2^31 from the low 32 bits of r, a pair that leaves unordered, or one whose extension falls outside [0, 262).

Serial arithmetic cannot detect an x that lies more than 2^31 SS_IDs from r: it extends such an x into the wrong epoch without error. A receiver therefore extends values relative to an r only while it can bound the number of SS_IDs between them below 2^31, and MUST re-establish the wrap epoch, in one of the ways above, after any gap that it cannot so bound, such as one that spans a rejoin of a multicast group or a reconnection of its MoQ session.
A receiver that has lost the source packet with SS_ID x, and holds no repair packet of the block that contains x, requests that block's repair by a FETCH of the absolute, inclusive Group range
on each repair track it requests from, where:

ul.li: S_prev is the SS_Start of the last block that the receiver has delimited that ends before x. When the receiver has delimited no such block, the first term is absent and the range is [ max(ext(x) - (K - 1), 0), ext(x) ];
ext(x) is x extended relative to ext(S_prev) when S_prev exists, and otherwise relative to the reference value r of the receiver's wrap epoch.

section.t: Repair Group IDs sit at block starts, so the range returns the repair of every block that starts within it, up to and including the block that contains x, and the last Group it returns is that block. The range is never empty: it always contains ext(x). A receiver that has not established the wrap epoch, or that may not extend x, has no range to request until it establishes one. A receiver that holds a repair packet of the block requests the one Group ext(SS_Start) instead.
The 32-bit wrap of SS_ID and SS_Start is that of . The extended SS_Start, and its use as a MoQ Group ID, are defined by this document, outside .

section.name: Block and Group Alignment
Single-Group Blocks (D = 1)
section.t: When D (Section 5.1) is 1, the FEC source packets of each MoQ Group of the source track, in SS_ID order, form one FEC block:
section.artwork: Group G: SS_ID s .. s+a-1 -> FEC block, SS_Start = s Group G+1: SS_ID s+a .. s+a+b-1 -> FEC block, SS_Start = s+a ...
section.t: A Group whose FEC source packets number more than K spans more than one block (Section 7.4). A block's repair objects form the repair-track Group whose Group ID is the block's extended SS_Start (Section 7.5), a number space unrelated to the source track's Group IDs.

section.name: Multi-Group Blocks (D > 1)
section.t: When the derived group count D is greater than 1, each FEC block spans D consecutive Groups:
section.artwork: Groups 0-3 (D=4): -> FEC block, SS_Start = s Groups 4-7 (D=4): -> FEC block, SS_Start = s + L ...
section.t: where L is the SSB_length of the first block. A block's repair objects are published after the last source object of the block's last Group.

section.name: Source Symbol Location
section.t: Under iso-ssbg1-v1, every FEC source packet carries a Source FEC Payload ID (Section 8.5), and a receiver takes each source symbol's SS_ID from that field on every path that delivers the packet with its trailer. Where a packaging profile delivers the protected packet without the trailer, the SS_ID is carried alongside it and the receiver takes it from there: on the MoQ path of Section 5.3 it is the FEC Source Info Object Property, which carries the same value under the same definition. The SS_ID advances by one per FEC source packet, modulo 2^32, in the order the publisher emits the packets ( Section C.5.2), and the blocks of an FEC instance are consecutive: each starts at the SS_ID that follows the last source symbol of its predecessor (Section 7.4).

A source symbol is located by range membership. It belongs to the block whose Repair FEC Payload ID (Section 7.1) carries an (SS_Start, SSB_length) such that the symbol's SS_ID lies in [SS_Start, SS_Start + SSB_length) under the serial arithmetic of Section 7.5, and its ESI is its serial distance from SS_Start:

No source symbol's block can be computed from its SS_ID alone, because blocks differ in length (Section 7.4), and this document defines no block number. A receiver holds a source symbol whose block it has not yet delimited, and places it when it accepts a repair packet of that block. Because consecutive FEC source packets carry consecutive SS_IDs, a lost source packet is visible as a missing SS_ID even before its block is delimited, and a run of SS_IDs that a receiver holds in full needs no repair, whatever its block boundaries.

An object that a packaging profile defines as carrying no source symbol -- for example, the in-band AL-FEC signaling object of Section 8 -- carries no SS_ID, has no ESI, and is not counted in K or in any block. This document defines no derivation of a source symbol's position from MoQ Group or Object IDs: on the mmtp packaging of , Object IDs are not positions in the FEC block, and a packaging profile whose source objects carry no Source FEC Payload ID needs a block profile of its own (Section 5.1).

Every transport path yields the same SS_ID for the same packet, because each path carries the same MMTP packet, so receivers MAY combine symbols from any transport path toward the same FEC block recovery. Within one FEC instance (Section 6.4.1), a receiver deduplicates source symbols by SS_ID and repair symbols by (SS_Start, RS_ID).

section.name: Encoder Constraints
section.t: For FEC block alignment to be deterministic, encoders MUST:

li.t: Use a fixed keyframe interval (constant GOP duration) within each FEC block. Variable GOP sizes (scene-cut adaptive keyframes) break the constant group duration from which the group count D of Section 5.1 is derived, and with it the block windows of Sections 8.1 and 8.2.

Signal the actual GOP duration and frame rate in the MoQ catalog: for mmtp-packaged tracks, the group duration in groupDurationMs (or groupDurationTicks where an exact tick count is needed), the keyframe cadence in keyframeIntervalMs (or keyframeIntervalTicks), and the frame rate in the framerate field ( Sections 4.4.2, 4.4.3 and 12.1). The ISO 23008-1 AL-FEC message has no field for either value ( Table C.3), so an encoder signals neither there, and a receiver takes neither from it.
If frame rate or GOP size changes mid-session, update the MoQ catalog and signal a manifest discontinuity for DASH/HLS.

Signal an interleave window that derives the intended group count: that is, an interleaveDepthMs for which Section 5.1 yields the intended D. The convention is interleaveDepthMs = round(D * group_duration_ms), which keeps the signaled value an integer even when the group duration is not an integer number of milliseconds (with one group per frame at 30 fps, D = 4 is signaled as round(4 x 33.33) = 133 ms).

section.name: Source FEC Payload ID and ATSC 3.0 Signed Region
section.t: Exactly one 4-byte Source FEC Payload ID (SS_ID; ffsrpts_flag = 0, so no FFSRP_TS, Section C.5.1) is appended at the END of each MMTP FEC source packet -- following the MMTP payload, outside the MMTP packet header -- with or without a keyframe overlay (Section 8.5.1). Per ATSC A/360 Section 5.2.2.5, the ATSC 3.0 Signed Application (A3SA) signing mechanism covers signaling messages and MA3 messages (packet type 0x2) but excludes asset packets (type 0x00 MPU and type 0x03 repair).

Neither nor carries the SS_ID inside the A3SA signed region. In particular the MMT hint sample does not: neither its ISO syntax ( Clause 8.3.2) nor the ATSC MMTHSampleATSC3 syntax ( Section 7.2.4.2.2.3) has a Source FEC Payload ID field, and hint samples travel as MPU-mode data units on the Asset's own packet_id ( Section 7.2.4.2.3), that is in asset packets, which A3SA does not sign. This document therefore defines no A3SA-authenticated FEC block assignment: block assignment taken from the trailing Source FEC Payload ID of an A3SA verified packet is unauthenticated. A receiver that requires authenticated FEC block assignment MUST obtain it from an integrity mechanism, other than A3SA signing, whose coverage includes the complete MMTP packet, the trailer included. The bc-provenance profile is not such a mechanism: its authenticated bytes exclude the Source FEC Payload ID ( Section 7.2.4).

For MoQ-only receivers (no A3SA verification), the trailing 4-byte Source FEC Payload ID remains the canonical identifier by which a source packet is placed in its block (Section 8.3). QUIC transport encryption provides equivalent integrity protection.

section.name: Overlay SS_ID Header Extension
section.t: When the catalog declares a keyframe overlay for a source track (Section 6.4), a source packet of that track carrying a Random Access Point fragment is a source symbol of two FEC instances. It carries its base SS_ID in the one Source FEC Payload ID trailer that every FEC source packet carries (Section 8.5), and its overlay SS_ID (Section 6.4.2) in an MMTP header extension ( Clause 9.2.3) of type 0x8B01:

A publisher that declares an overlay MUST carry this extension as the header extension, with X = 1, of exactly the source packets that it includes in the overlay instance, that is the packets on which it sets RAP_flag (Section 6.4.2), and of no other packet of the track. An MMTP packet carries at most one header extension ( Clause 9.2.3), so the RAP packets of a track under an overlay carry no other MMTP header extension, and a publisher that needs another header extension on those packets cannot use the overlay for that track. specifies no particular header extension and no registry of header extension types; this document uses the type 0x8B01 for the overlay SS_ID (Section 15.1).

The trailer is never more than one Source FEC Payload ID. On a packet with or without the extension, the last four bytes are the base SS_ID, as Section C.4.2 places it, so a receiver that does not implement overlays locates the trailer and the payload as on any other packet, stepping over the extension by its Length field. The extension lies inside the MMTP packet header, so it is part of the protected packet of both instances (Section 7.3), which protect one identical source symbol. The permission of Clause 9.2.3 to discard a header extension therefore extends only to a receiver's own processing: a node that forwards the packet MUST NOT remove or alter the extension. A RAP packet recovered by either instance carries its overlay SS_ID, so a receiver MAY place a RAP packet that the base instance recovered into the overlay block that the extension locates; Section 7.3 states why the converse requires the packet's base SS_ID.

A receiver that implements overlays takes a packet's overlay SS_ID from this extension and from nothing else. It MUST NOT feed the overlay decoder a source packet that lacks the extension, whatever its RAP_flag, or one whose extension has a Length other than 4, and MUST NOT infer an overlay SS_ID from RAP_flag, from the packet's position, or from its base SS_ID.

A source track has at most one overlay (Section 6.3.4, rule 10) because a source packet has one header extension, and so carries one overlay SS_ID; relaxing that bound would be a revision of this document and a change to the source packet layout, not a catalog-only change.

The overlay is declared only by the catalog. A publisher MUST NOT describe the overlay's repair flow in an AL-FEC message ( Section 8.3): the message identifies an FEC source flow by packet_id ( Clause C.6.3) and cannot describe the RAP subset that the overlay protects, so a receiver that consumes the flow without the catalog uses the base instance alone. An overlay is defined only without FFSRP_TS: a publisher MUST NOT declare an overlay for a source track whose FEC source or repair packets carry FFSRP_TS (ffsrpts_flag = 1, Section C.5.1), and the extension carries an SS_ID alone.
Section 8.5 applies to the overlay SS_ID as to the base one: A3SA signing authenticates neither, and a receiver that requires authenticated block assignment treats each as Section 8.5 requires.

section.name: Interleaving
section.t: Interleaving spreads source symbols across time to protect against burst loss. The interleave window (Interleave Depth, in milliseconds) sets the time span of each source block; the number of consecutive groups in one block follows as D (Section 5.1). With D = 4, symbols from 4 consecutive groups are grouped into one source block:
section.artwork: Groups: M0 M1 M2 M3 M4 M5 M6 M7 | | | | | | | | D=4: [--- Block 0 ---] [--- Block 1 ---] S0 S1 S2 S3 S4 S5 S6 S7 | | Block 0 Repair: Block 1 Repair: R0, R1 R2, R3
section.t: A burst loss affecting M1-M2 loses symbols S1,S2 from Block 0. With P >= 2 repair symbols, Block 0 can still be recovered.
Publishers SHOULD choose the interleave window based on:

ul.li: Expected burst loss duration
Acceptable recovery latency
Available bandwidth for repair overhead

section.t: The receiver's block-abandonment timeout -- how long it waits for a block's source and repair symbols before declaring the block unrecoverable -- follows the ISO receiver-buffer model Section 11.2. The timer is anchored at the timestamp ts of the first source or repair packet of the block when the receiver received that packet, not at block creation or the first repair receipt. A block whose first packet the receiver did not receive is one that it first learns of from a later signal -- a later source or repair packet of the block, a packet of a successor block, or a FETCH response that covers the block (Section 7.5) -- and its ts is the arrival time of that signal. The base FEC deadline is:
Here interleaveDepthMs is the complete first-to-last block span of Section 5.1, which already bounds source and repair production at the media cadence and their serialization.

Implementations MUST NOT derive a full-block span or FEC deadline from K, from D, from a per-symbol interval, or by a multiplier: the block span is interleaveDepthMs, and a deadline adds interleaveDepthMs and, where used, reorderToleranceMs, each exactly once.

A receiver uses the catalog reorderToleranceMs allowance, when present, for network jitter, one-way delay, reordering, and local processing before abandoning the block. That allowance is additive to the base span and MUST be applied exactly once. If the field is absent, Section 5.1 applies. At the resulting deadline, the receiver moves the block onward and attempts FEC processing according to its buffering model. What a receiver of a multicast or AMT leg does with a block that is still unrecovered at that deadline -- unicast repair, a stall, or concealment -- is specified in Section 11.4.

The code is systematic (Section 4.1): a receiver plays source objects on arrival, and the window adds latency only when a lossy leg forces it to wait for recovery. The "Recovery Latency" column below is that worst-case budget.
Typical values (D follows from the group duration):

section.name: Priority and Congestion
section.t: Priorities in this document are expressed in the MoQ Transport priority scale : an 8-bit value (0-255) in which a numerically LOWER value is delivered with HIGHER precedence. Repair tracks SHOULD use a numerically greater (lower-precedence) priority than the source tracks they protect, so that repair data is dropped first under congestion. The RECOMMENDED assignment places a repair track's priority value at least 64 above its source track's (e.g. repair 240 against a source track at the common default of 128):

Layer priorities and the layer-0 default follow Section 6.3.4, rule 3, so under congestion the highest layer is shed first and a receiver degrades through its layer set in order; a keyframe overlay's priority is independent of that order (Section 6.4.1).
Publishers and relays convey these priorities through the priority fields and scheduling rules of (subscriber and publisher priority); QUIC itself defines no wire-visible stream priority mechanism.
Under congestion, this priority separation ensures:

ol.li: Source media is preserved as long as possible
Repair overhead is gracefully shed
Receivers degrade to QUIC retransmission when FEC is unavailable

section.t: On a multicast or AMT leg, the priorities of on-demand unicast repair requests are set by Section 11.4.5.

section.name: Hybrid Unicast and Multicast Delivery
section.t: This FEC mechanism is designed to support hybrid delivery architectures where the same media stream is delivered via multiple transport paths simultaneously. Multicast delivery paths, TreeDN integration, and the transport hierarchy (all Section 3) are defined in ; this section covers FEC-specific considerations for hybrid delivery.

section.name: Multicast and AMT Delivery
section.t: IP multicast (including Source-Specific Multicast per ) and Automatic Multicast Tunneling (AMT per ) provide efficient one-to-many delivery but are inherently unreliable. FEC enables receivers to recover from packet loss without retransmission:

ul.li: Native SSM: Receivers join multicast group directly
AMT Tunneling: Receivers without native multicast connect via AMT relays discovered through DRIAD ()
TreeDN Distribution: Hierarchical multicast trees per , with FEC protection at each hop

section.t: The same MoQ objects (source and repair) can be transmitted over both unicast (QUIC/WebTransport) and multicast (UDP/SSM/AMT) paths. Receivers on reliable unicast paths can skip FEC decoding (Section 3), while receivers on lossy multicast paths use FEC for recovery and apply the receiver repair policy of Section 11.4 to any block that FEC does not recover.
